extra_info: In China, the General Secretary is the top leader of the Communist Party of China (CPC), a party position rather than, by itself, the head of government. The same person commonly also serves as China's president and chair of the Central Military Commission; these are distinct offices.
paragraphs: At a civics exhibit, a student reads a panel about China's political institutions. It explains that the General Secretary {{mask_1}} leads the Communist Party of China (CPC) is the party's top leader. A guide {{mask_2}} Lin asks about the title points to a chart of the party's central bodies. Researchers {{mask_3}} study the CPC distinguish party leadership from state offices. The display includes interviews with historians with {{mask_4}} visitors can discuss changes in the role over time. A lecturer {{mask_5}} has written about these institutions says that the title refers to a party position.

Lin's class discusses how the role relates to other offices. The person {{mask_6}} the party elects as General Secretary leads its Central Committee. Students also read an interview with an adviser {{mask_7}} the General Secretary consults on institutional matters. They read a report by an analyst {{mask_8}} the teacher interviewed about how party and state institutions differ. A visitor {{mask_9}} works at a research institute offers an example from a recent history project. A historian {{mask_10}} contributes to the exhibit explains why each office has its own formal responsibilities.

The next panel introduces the Central Military Commission. It describes the commission as a party and state institution concerned with military leadership. A scholar {{mask_11}} the students invited to speak explains that the commission's chairmanship is a separate office, even when held by the same person. A delegate {{mask_12}} attended a public lecture asks how these roles are presented in official biographies. A researcher {{mask_13}} studies political terminology recommends checking which office a source is referring to. Another researcher {{mask_14}} contributes to the exhibit has prepared a glossary for the class.

For a group assignment, Lin and her classmates compare several biographies and news reports. They consult an editor {{mask_15}} they met at the exhibit about how titles are translated. A student {{mask_16}} organizes their notes labels each reference as a party or state office. The instructor to {{mask_17}} they submit their draft suggests adding a note about the distinction. Readers {{mask_18}} want to understand the institutional context can use the glossary. In their presentation, they cite a speaker {{mask_19}} the guide referred to earlier and identify the source of each statement. The visitors, many of {{mask_20}} have different questions about the system, leave with a clearer understanding of the title.
